short: A large professional investor, such as a mutual fund, bank, insurer or foreign fund, that gets its own reserved slice of Indian IPOs.
kid: Imagine a bakery saving one big tray of cakes just for the biggest, most careful buyers, like school canteens. Those big careful buyers get their own tray.
detail: A qualified institutional buyer (QIB) is an institution that SEBI's ICDR regulations treat as able to judge an investment on its own: mutual funds, scheduled commercial banks, insurers, pension and provident funds, foreign portfolio investors (other than individuals, corporate bodies and family offices), alternative investment funds and similar bodies. In a book-built IPO by a company that meets the profitability track record, not more than 50% of the net offer goes to QIBs, under the rules as of 2025; a loss-making issuer must give QIBs at least 75%. Up to 60% of the QIB portion can be placed with anchor investors a day before the issue opens. QIB demand is watched closely because it signals what informed money thinks of the price. QIBs cannot withdraw or lower bids. Do not confuse a QIB (the investor) with a QIP, a qualified institutional placement (a way of raising money).
example: Say ABC Ltd, a profitable company, offers ₹1,000 crore of shares. QIBs can get up to ₹500 crore (50%), of which up to ₹300 crore (60% of ₹500 crore) can go to anchor investors. If other QIBs then bid ₹20,000 crore for the remaining ₹200 crore, the QIB portion (excluding anchors) is reported as subscribed 100 times.

short: An individual, company or trust bidding above the retail limit in an Indian IPO without being an institution; the so-called high-net-worth (HNI) category.
kid: Some people want just a few sweets, and big shops want boxes and boxes. In between are grown-ups who want a big bag for their own family, and they get their own line.
detail: Non-institutional investors (NIIs) are IPO applicants who are not QIBs and who bid for more than ₹2 lakh: wealthy individuals, HUFs, companies, trusts and NRIs, under SEBI's ICDR rules as of 2025. A profitable issuer must reserve at least 15% of the net offer for them. Since April 2022 the NII portion is split: one-third for bids between ₹2 lakh and ₹10 lakh (small NII, or sNII) and two-thirds for bids above ₹10 lakh (big NII, or bNII). Allotment is no longer proportionate to bid size: when a slice is oversubscribed, shares go by lottery, each winner getting the minimum NII application. That change largely ended the old trick of borrowing heavily to place giant bids. NIIs, like QIBs, cannot withdraw or lower bids. A common confusion: 'HNI' here is a bid-size bucket, not a test of the applicant's wealth.
example: Say ABC Ltd's IPO has ₹150 crore for NIIs. The sNII slice gets ₹50 crore (one-third) and the bNII slice ₹100 crore (two-thirds). If bNII bids total ₹5,000 crore, that slice is subscribed 50 times, and most bNII applicants will get nothing in the lottery.

short: An individual who applies for shares in an Indian IPO up to the retail limit, ₹2 lakh under the rules as of 2025.
kid: When the cake is cut at a party, the grown-ups make sure a big part is saved for the children. Every child in line gets a fair chance at a slice.
detail: A retail individual investor (RII) is an individual, including an eligible NRI or an HUF applying through its karta, who bids in an IPO for shares worth no more than ₹2 lakh, under SEBI's ICDR rules as of 2025. A company meeting the profitability track record must reserve at least 35% of the net offer for RIIs; a loss-making issuer can give them at most 10%. Retail bidders may bid at the 'cut-off' price, accepting whatever final price is set within the band, and they can modify or cancel bids before the issue closes. If the retail book is oversubscribed, the rule is to give as many applicants as possible one minimum lot each, chosen by lottery, rather than pro-rata slices. The common confusion is that applying for more lots raises your odds: in a heavily oversubscribed issue, each application has roughly the same chance of one lot.
example: Say ABC Ltd's IPO sets aside 2 lakh retail lots, and 20 lakh valid retail applications arrive. Each applicant has about a 1 in 10 chance of winning one lot. If a lot is 40 shares at ₹350, a winner pays ₹14,000.

short: A sale of shares to selected investors shortly before a company's IPO, usually to secure early backing and shrink the public offer.
kid: Before the big toy sale opens to everyone, the shop lets a few friends buy some toys early. Then fewer toys are left for the big sale.
detail: A pre-IPO placement is a private issue of shares that a company makes before filing its red herring prospectus, under a plan already disclosed in its draft prospectus. Under SEBI's ICDR rules as of 2025, its size cannot exceed 20% of the fresh issue, the amount raised is deducted from the fresh issue, and the deal must be reported to the exchanges within 24 hours. The price is often close to the expected IPO band, so it works as an early signal of valuation. More loosely, 'pre-IPO round' also means any late private funding round raised a year or two before listing. Shares bought by non-promoters before the IPO are typically locked in for six months after listing, so watch for selling pressure when that lock-in ends. Do not confuse it with the anchor book, which is part of the IPO itself.
example: Say ABC Ltd plans a ₹1,000 crore fresh issue and places ₹150 crore of shares with two funds before filing its red herring prospectus. The fresh issue in the IPO shrinks to ₹850 crore, and the ₹150 crore is within the 20% cap of ₹200 crore.

short: A sale of existing shares by current owners, such as founders or the government; the money goes to the sellers, not the company.
kid: If your friend sells you one of her old toys, the coins go to your friend, not to the toy shop. The shop gets nothing new.
detail: An offer for sale (OFS) is the sale of shares that already exist, by promoters, private equity funds or the government, rather than the issue of new ones. It appears in two forms. Inside an IPO, the OFS portion sits alongside any fresh issue: fresh-issue money funds the company, while OFS money goes straight to the sellers. Separately, SEBI's stock-exchange OFS window lets promoters and other large shareholders of listed companies sell big blocks quickly: the seller gives a day's notice and sets a minimum (floor) price, non-retail investors bid on the first day and retail investors on the next, with at least 10% reserved for retail, under the rules as of 2025. The government often uses this route for disinvestment. The common confusion is to read a big IPO size as fresh capital for growth: if it is mostly OFS, the company itself receives nothing.
example: Say ABC Ltd's ₹1,200 crore IPO has a ₹300 crore fresh issue and a ₹900 crore OFS. The company receives only ₹300 crore (before expenses), while the selling shareholders take home ₹900 crore. Three-quarters of the IPO is simply existing owners cashing out.

short: A listed company issuing new shares, or rights to buy them later, to a chosen group of investors instead of the public, with shareholder approval.
kid: Instead of selling your new stickers to the whole class, you sell some only to two friends you picked. The class has to agree first.
detail: A preferential allotment is an issue of equity shares, fully convertible securities or warrants by a listed company to a select group of investors, governed by Chapter V of SEBI's ICDR regulations. It needs a special resolution of shareholders. To protect existing holders, the issue price cannot be below a floor based on volume-weighted average prices; for frequently traded shares this is the higher of the 90-trading-day and 10-trading-day averages before the relevant date, under the rules as of 2025. Allotted shares are locked in, longer for promoters than for others. With warrants, at least 25% of the price is paid upfront and the rest on conversion within 18 months. It is quicker and cheaper than a public offer, but it dilutes everyone else, and a large allotment to promoters at a low price is a classic governance red flag. Unlike a QIP, investors here need not be institutions.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 9 crore shares and allots 1 crore new shares at ₹250 each to two funds, raising ₹250 crore. The new investors now own 10% of the enlarged 10 crore shares, and every existing holder's stake shrinks by a tenth: a 20% holder drops to 18%.

short: Removing a company's shares from a stock exchange so they can no longer be traded there, usually after the controlling owners buy out other shareholders.
kid: Imagine a toy that everyone could swap at the playground. One day the owner buys all the pieces back and takes it home, so nobody can swap it there any more.
detail: Delisting removes a company's shares from trading on an exchange. In voluntary delisting, the promoter offers to buy out public shareholders under SEBI's Delisting Regulations, 2021. The classic method is reverse book building: shareholders tender shares at prices at or above a floor price, and the discovered price is the one at which the promoter's holding would reach 90% of the company. The promoter may accept it, reject it and keep the company listed, or make a counter-offer. Under the rules as of 2025, a fixed-price route with a premium of at least 15% over the floor is also allowed for frequently traded shares. Compulsory delisting is a penalty imposed by the exchange, after which promoters must buy shares at an independently set fair value and face a 10-year bar from the market. Delisting is not the same as a trading suspension, which is temporary.
example: Say promoters own 80% of ABC Ltd's 10 crore shares and set a floor price of ₹400. To reach 90% they need 1 crore of the 2 crore public shares. If tenders at ₹480 or below add up to exactly 1 crore shares, ₹480 is the discovered price, and accepting it costs the promoters ₹480 crore.

short: The part of a stock exchange where contracts on future prices of shares and indices, called futures and options, are traded.
kid: Some children swap real toys. Others swap promises, like 'next Friday I will give you my car for your ball.' This is the corner of the playground for swapping promises.
detail: The F&O segment is the exchange segment for equity derivatives: futures, which oblige both sides to trade at a set price on expiry, and options, which give the buyer a right but not an obligation. In India it is dominated by NSE, with BSE a growing rival, and by index options in particular, so its notional turnover dwarfs cash trading. Index contracts are cash-settled, while stock F&O contracts have been physically settled since 2019, meaning positions open at expiry turn into actual share delivery. Only stocks meeting SEBI's size and liquidity criteria are eligible. SEBI studies have found that roughly nine in ten individual F&O traders lose money, which led to tighter rules from November 2024, including larger contract sizes and fewer weekly expiries. The common confusion is to treat F&O as a cheap way to own shares: it is leveraged and time-limited, and losses can exceed the margin posted.
example: Say an index trades at 20,000 and its futures lot is 75 units. One futures contract controls 75 × 20,000 = ₹15 lakh of exposure for an initial margin of perhaps ₹1.8 lakh. A 2% fall in the index costs the buyer ₹30,000, a sixth of that margin.

short: The fixed number of units in one derivatives contract, or the minimum batch of shares you must bid for in an IPO.
kid: Some sweets are sold only in packets of ten. You cannot buy three; you buy one packet, or two, or more.
detail: Lot size is the minimum tradable quantity of an exchange-traded contract. In India's F&O segment each contract covers a fixed number of units of the underlying share or index, set by the exchange so that the contract value stays within a SEBI band; from November 2024 SEBI raised the minimum value of index derivative contracts to ₹15 lakh at introduction, under the rules as of 2025. Exchanges revise lot sizes periodically as prices move, so check the current exchange circular rather than memorising a number. In IPOs the 'market lot' or minimum bid lot is the smallest block of shares an applicant can bid for, sized to keep one lot affordable for retail investors. In the cash market, demat shares trade in lots of one. A common error is to read profit per unit as profit per trade: always multiply by the lot size and the number of lots.
example: Say an index future has a lot size of 75 and the index rises from 20,000 to 20,200. A trader holding 2 lots gains 200 × 75 × 2 = ₹30,000, not ₹200.
formula: Contract value = Lot size × Price of the underlying

short: A daily list of stocks with so many open futures and options bets that traders may only reduce, not add to, positions.
kid: When too many children crowd onto one slide, the teacher says, 'No more getting on. You can only climb off.' The slide opens again when the crowd gets smaller.
detail: Every F&O stock has a market-wide position limit (MWPL), the maximum open interest the system allows across all traders. When open interest crosses 95% of the MWPL, the stock enters the ban period: no fresh positions may be created and traders can only reduce existing ones, under the rules as of 2025. The ban lifts once open interest falls below 80% of the MWPL. Anyone who increases a position during the ban is penalised. The MWPL was long the lower of 20% of non-promoter shares and 30 times average daily cash-market volume; in 2025 SEBI changed it to the lower of 15% of free float and 65 times average daily delivery value, and began measuring open interest on a delta-adjusted, future-equivalent basis. The ban does not stop trading in the shares themselves, and it says nothing about the company's fundamentals, though such stocks are often volatile.
example: Say a stock's MWPL is 10 crore shares. If open interest reaches 9.6 crore shares, above the 95% trigger of 9.5 crore, the stock enters the ban. It leaves only after open interest falls below 8 crore shares, 80% of the limit.
formula: MWPL utilisation = Open interest across all traders / Market-wide position limit

short: The upfront deposit an exchange requires on futures and options, worked out by testing how much a whole portfolio could lose in one bad day.
kid: Before you borrow a friend's bike, you leave your toy car with them. If the bike gets scratched, they keep the car to fix it. Bigger risk, bigger toy left behind.
detail: SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk) is a margining method created by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange in 1988 and used by Indian clearing corporations for F&O. It runs a portfolio through a set of scenarios, typically 16 combinations of price and volatility moves, and sets the margin at the worst one-day loss, so offsetting positions such as a hedged futures-and-options pair need less margin than the gross positions would. In India the total initial margin is SPAN plus an exposure margin, an extra buffer set as a percentage of contract value to cover risks the scenarios miss. Brokers usually show the two as one F&O margin figure. Margin is a good-faith deposit, not a cost and not the maximum loss: if prices move against you, you must top up through daily mark-to-market payments.
example: Say one lot of index futures is worth ₹15 lakh, SPAN requires ₹1.2 lakh and exposure margin is 2% of contract value, or ₹30,000. The trader must keep ₹1.5 lakh with the broker before opening the position.
formula: Initial F&O margin = SPAN margin + Exposure margin

short: A SEBI rule that traders keep enough deposit with their broker to cover their biggest position at any moment, checked by surprise intraday snapshots.
kid: Before, you could promise to pay for lots of sweets as long as you paid by evening. Now the shopkeeper peeks into your pocket at surprise times, and you must have enough every time.
detail: Peak margin is SEBI's rule that the margin a client has deposited must cover the highest margin requirement reached during the day, not just the end-of-day position. Clearing corporations take at least four random snapshots of every client's positions each day, and the largest requirement counts. It was phased in from December 2020, rising from 25% to 100% of the requirement by September 2021. Before it, brokers often gave intraday traders 20 to 50 times leverage, because positions were squared off before the end-of-day check. Under the rules as of 2025, cash-market traders must deposit the full upfront margin, at least 20% of trade value, before trading, which caps intraday leverage at about five times, and brokers are penalised for short collection. The common confusion is to blame one broker for 'cutting leverage': the limit is regulatory and applies to every broker.
example: Say a trader has ₹1 lakh. Before peak margin, a broker might have allowed ₹20 lakh of intraday buying (20 times). If the stock's upfront margin is 20%, she can now buy at most ₹1 lakh / 20% = ₹5 lakh.
formula: Maximum position allowed = Margin available / Upfront margin rate

short: The total face value of derivative contracts traded, counting the full value of the shares or index behind each contract, not the money actually paid.
kid: If you rent a big toy castle for one coin a day, you only paid one coin, even though the castle is worth a whole jar of coins. Counting the whole castle makes the number look huge.
detail: Notional turnover adds up the full contract value of every derivatives trade: for futures, quantity times price; for options, quantity times strike plus premium on NSE's method. Premium turnover counts only the option premiums that actually change hands. The gap is enormous in India, where index options dominate: notional F&O turnover has at times been hundreds of times cash-market turnover, while premium turnover is a small fraction of notional. Claims that India has the world's largest derivatives market usually rest on contract counts or notional figures, which overstate the money at risk. SEBI and analysts increasingly cite premium turnover, or delta-adjusted figures, to judge real activity, and exchange fees on options are charged on premium. The common confusion is to treat ₹100 lakh crore of notional options turnover as ₹100 lakh crore of money traded.
example: Say a trader buys 10 lots of index call options with a lot size of 75, a strike of 20,000 and a premium of ₹100. On NSE's method, notional turnover is 750 × (20,000 + 100) = ₹1,50,75,000, about ₹1.51 crore, but premium turnover is only 750 × ₹100 = ₹75,000.
formula: Futures notional = Quantity × Price; Options notional (NSE) = Quantity × (Strike + Premium); Premium turnover = Quantity × Premium

short: The part of a stock exchange where shares themselves are bought and sold, for delivery or same-day trading, as opposed to futures and options.
kid: This is the shop where you actually buy the toy and take it home. Next door is a corner where children only make promises about toys.
detail: The equity cash segment, called the capital market segment on NSE, is where shares, ETFs and similar securities change hands outright. A buyer who keeps the shares receives them in their demat account on settlement, which in India has been T+1 for all stocks since January 2023. Traders can also buy and sell the same stock within a day (intraday); those trades are netted and only the difference settles. Cash turnover is the best gauge of genuine demand for shares, and delivery volume, the part not squared off intraday, is watched as a sign of conviction. In India, cash turnover is a tiny fraction of F&O notional turnover, so comparing the two raw numbers says more about how derivatives are counted than about real money. Do not confuse 'cash segment' with paying in cash: all trades settle electronically through the clearing corporation.
example: Say an investor buys 100 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹1,500 on a Monday in the cash segment. She pays ₹1,50,000 (plus charges) and the shares reach her demat account on Tuesday, under T+1 settlement.

short: The rule that a share trade is completed one working day after the trade day, when the buyer gets shares and the seller gets money.
kid: You swap stickers with a friend today, but the stickers and coins actually change hands tomorrow. One sleep, and the swap is done.
detail: T+1 means a trade done on day T is settled on the next trading day: the clearing corporation delivers shares to the buyer's demat account and funds to the seller. India moved from T+2 to T+1 in phases between February 2022 and January 2023, starting with the smallest stocks, making it one of the first major markets on a one-day cycle; the US followed in May 2024. Rolling settlement means every trading day has its own settlement, unlike the old weekly account periods. Shorter cycles cut counterparty risk and free up capital faster, but give foreign investors and custodians less time to arrange funds and currency. An optional T+0 cycle has also run alongside since 2024. The count uses trading days, so a Friday trade settles on Monday, and a holiday pushes settlement back.
example: Say you sell 50 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹800 on a Thursday. Under T+1 the ₹40,000 (before charges) reaches your broker on Friday; under the old T+2 it would have arrived on Monday.
formula: Settlement date = Trade date + 1 trading day

short: The daily ceiling and floor an exchange sets on a stock's price, beyond which it cannot trade that day.
kid: The teacher says a swing may go only so high and only so low today. If it reaches the top, it stops there until tomorrow.
detail: A circuit, or price band, caps how far a stock's price can move in a session relative to the previous close. Indian exchanges assign bands of 2%, 5%, 10% or 20% to stocks outside the F&O segment, tightening them for volatile or surveillance stocks; F&O stocks instead have wider dynamic bands that can be relaxed during the day, under the rules as of 2025. When a stock hits its upper circuit there are buyers but almost no sellers, and it can stay 'locked' there; at the lower circuit sellers queue with no buyers, which can trap investors for days. These stock-level limits are separate from market-wide circuit breakers, which halt all trading when the Nifty or Sensex moves 10%, 15% or 20%. A stock repeatedly hitting upper circuit is not proof of quality; thin trading and operator activity often lie behind it.
example: Say ABC Ltd closed at ₹200 and has a 5% band. Today it can trade only between ₹190 and ₹210. If it hits ₹210 with a wall of buy orders and few sellers, it is said to be locked in the upper circuit.
formula: Upper circuit = Previous close × (1 + Band %); Lower circuit = Previous close × (1 - Band %)

short: An exchange watch-list that puts extra trading curbs on stocks showing unusual price or volume swings, to cool speculation.
kid: When one swing in the park gets pushed too high and too fast, the teacher stands beside it and makes children take slower turns. The swing is fine; the crowd is just too wild.
detail: The Additional Surveillance Measure (ASM) framework, run jointly by SEBI and the exchanges since 2018, shortlists stocks using objective, market-based tests such as high-low price variation, close-to-close moves, client concentration, volume spikes and valuation, and then applies graded curbs. There are short-term stages (I and II) and long-term stages (I to IV). Typical measures include 100% upfront margin, a tighter price band and, in higher long-term stages, trade-for-trade settlement. Stocks move in and out automatically as the parameters are reviewed. ASM is a cooling-off tool, not a finding of wrongdoing by the company, but it reduces leverage and liquidity and often slows a speculative rally. Do not confuse it with GSM, which targets stocks whose price looks out of line with weak fundamentals rather than just unusual trading behaviour.
example: Say ABC Ltd's shares jump from ₹100 to ₹260 in a month on thin volumes and it enters an ASM stage that requires 100% margin. A trader who could earlier buy ₹5 lakh of the stock with ₹1 lakh must now put up the full ₹5 lakh.

short: A tougher exchange watch-list for stocks whose prices look out of line with the company's weak finances, with curbs that rise in stages.
kid: If a tiny paper boat is being sold as if it were a real ship, the grown-ups step in. First they slow the selling down, and if it keeps going, they slow it even more.
detail: The Graded Surveillance Measure (GSM) framework, introduced by SEBI and the exchanges in 2017, targets stocks whose price is not in line with the company's financial health, typically small companies with low earnings, net worth or book value but sharp price rises. Shortlisted stocks are placed in stages with escalating curbs: trade-for-trade settlement with 100% margin, an additional surveillance deposit of 100% or more of trade value held by the exchange for months, and at the higher stages trading allowed only once a week. Stocks are reviewed periodically and can move up, down or out. GSM aims to protect investors from manipulated or speculative small caps, and the deposit makes buying such stocks very costly. The key difference from ASM is the trigger: GSM compares price with fundamentals, whereas ASM reacts to unusual price and volume behaviour.
example: Say ABC Ltd, with tiny profits, is placed in a GSM stage requiring an additional surveillance deposit of 100% of trade value. A buyer of ₹2 lakh of its shares must pay ₹2 lakh for the shares and park another ₹2 lakh with the exchange, ₹4 lakh in all.

short: A category where every trade must end in actual delivery of shares, so buying and selling the same day cannot cancel out.
kid: Usually, if you swap a marble away and get it back before home time, nothing changes. In this game, every swap really happens, so each marble must truly move every time.
detail: In the trade-for-trade (T2T) segment, each trade is settled on its own by delivery: obligations from buying and selling the same stock on the same day are not netted, so intraday trading is effectively impossible. If you sell shares you do not already hold, you face short delivery and an exchange auction, with penalties. Exchanges move stocks here as a surveillance measure, typically for stocks in ASM or GSM stages, those with abnormal price moves, or companies with compliance lapses. On NSE such stocks trade in the BE (or BZ) series instead of EQ; on BSE they sit in the T group, or XT for BSE-only stocks. T2T stocks usually also carry tight price bands. A common misreading is to see the BE tag as a sign of corporate fraud: it signals speculative trading risk, not a verdict on the business.
example: Say a T2T stock trades at ₹50. You buy 100 shares in the morning for ₹5,000 and sell 100 in the afternoon at ₹52 for ₹5,200. The trades are not netted: the shares you bought are credited only after the sale's T+1 delivery deadline, so you cannot deliver on the sale, which goes to auction with penalties that can exceed the ₹200 gain.

short: BSE's labels, such as A, B, T, X and Z, that sort listed stocks by size, liquidity, settlement type or compliance record.
kid: A teacher sorts toys into boxes: big popular toys in one, ordinary toys in another, and toys whose owners never follow the rules in a special box. The label tells you which box a toy is in.
detail: BSE classifies its listed equities into groups. Group A holds the larger, more liquid companies, selected on criteria such as market capitalisation, turnover and trading frequency; most other regular stocks sit in Group B. Group T holds stocks settled on a trade-for-trade basis as a surveillance measure. Group X covers companies listed only on BSE (with XT for those in trade-for-trade), while M and MT cover SME-platform stocks. Group Z holds companies that have failed to meet listing obligations, not resolved investor complaints, or lack depository connectivity. Classification is reviewed periodically, so stocks move between groups. For a new investor, Z is the important flag: it signals a compliance problem and usually thin, risky trading. Do not read A as a quality or 'buy' rating; it is about size and liquidity, not valuation.
example: Say XYZ Ltd, a hypothetical B-group company, misses its quarterly filings and is moved to Group Z, with its price band cut to 5%. From a previous close of ₹40, it can then trade only between ₹38 and ₹42 in a day.

short: SEBI's rulebook for listed companies in India, covering what they must disclose, when, and how their boards must be run.
kid: When you join a club, you promise to share news quickly and play by the club's rules. These are the club rules for companies that anyone can own a little piece of.
detail: The SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, known as LODR, set the continuing duties of companies whose securities are listed on Indian exchanges. They require quarterly financial results within 45 days of quarter-end (60 days for annual audited results), prompt disclosure of material events under Regulation 30, and governance standards: minimum numbers of independent directors, audit and nomination committees, shareholder approval of material related-party transactions, and a sustainability report for the largest companies. Under the rules as of 2025, board decisions must be disclosed within 30 minutes of the meeting ending, and the largest listed companies must confirm or deny market rumours. Breaches lead to exchange fines, freezing of promoter holdings and, in extreme cases, suspension. LODR covers life after listing; the rules for raising capital sit in the ICDR regulations.
example: Say ABC Ltd's quarter ends on 30 June. Under LODR it must publish results by 14 August, 45 days later, and if its board approves a dividend at a meeting ending at 3:00 pm, the exchange must be told by 3:30 pm.

aliases: Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers
hl: substantial acquisition of shares and takeovers
short: SEBI's takeover rules, which force anyone buying a big stake or control in a listed company to offer to buy shares from the public too.
kid: If a new child wants to become the boss of the sandcastle team, she must first offer to buy every other child's spade at a fair price. Then no one is left out.
detail: The SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, the Takeover Code, protect minority shareholders when control of a listed company changes. Under the rules as of 2025, an acquirer whose holding, with persons acting in concert, reaches 25% of voting rights, or who acquires control at any level, must make an open offer to buy at least a further 26% of the company from public shareholders. Holders between 25% and 75% may 'creep' up by at most 5% a financial year without an offer. The offer price must be at least the highest of several benchmarks, including the negotiated deal price and recent market averages, so public holders share in any control premium. The code also requires disclosure when holdings cross 5% and on each 2% change after that. A common confusion: an open offer is an invitation, not an obligation to sell.
example: Say an acquirer buys a 26% stake in ABC Ltd, which has 10 crore shares, from its founders at ₹300 a share. Crossing 25% triggers an open offer for a further 26%, or 2.6 crore shares; at ₹300 a share, the offer could cost up to ₹780 crore if fully accepted.

aliases: Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements
hl: issue of capital and disclosure requirements
short: SEBI's rulebook for how Indian companies raise money from investors through IPOs, rights issues, QIPs and preferential allotments, and what they must disclose.
kid: Before a lemonade stand asks friends for help to grow, there are rules: say clearly what the coins will be used for, and let everyone ask fairly. These are those rules.
detail: The SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, known as ICDR, govern how companies raise capital from the market in India. They cover IPOs and follow-on offers, rights issues, preferential allotments, qualified institutional placements and bonus issues. They set eligibility tests, such as the profitability track record for a standard IPO, the contents of the draft and red herring prospectus, pricing rules, allocation among QIBs, NIIs and retail investors, anchor investors, and lock-in of promoter shares. Under the rules as of 2025, promoters must keep at least 20% of post-issue capital locked in for 18 months after an IPO, longer when proceeds fund capital expenditure. ICDR is amended often, so check the latest version. Do not confuse it with LODR, which governs obligations after listing, or with the Companies Act, the underlying corporate law.
example: Say ABC Ltd will have 10 crore shares after its IPO. ICDR's minimum promoter contribution means at least 2 crore shares, 20% of post-issue capital, stay locked in for 18 months, so promoters cannot sell that stake right after listing.

short: SEBI's rules that bar anyone with important unreleased company information from trading on it, and set controls on insiders' share dealings.
kid: If you secretly saw which box has the prize, it would be unfair to swap boxes with friends before they know. These rules say you must wait until everyone knows.
detail: The SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, bar insiders from trading in a listed company's securities while holding unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI), such as results, dividends, mergers or major orders, and bar anyone from passing such information on except for legitimate purposes. 'Insider' covers directors and employees, connected persons and anyone who has UPSI. Companies must keep a code of conduct, a structured digital database of who received UPSI, trading window closures and pre-clearance of larger trades by designated persons; insiders may trade under a pre-disclosed trading plan. Under the rules as of 2025, promoters, directors and designated persons must disclose trades above ₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter within two trading days. Penalties under the SEBI Act reach ₹25 crore or three times the profit made, whichever is higher. Trading while holding UPSI is presumed to be insider trading unless the insider proves a permitted defence.
example: Say a finance manager at ABC Ltd learns before results that profit has doubled, and buys 2,000 shares at ₹500 (₹10 lakh). After the results the price jumps to ₹650, a ₹3 lakh gain. SEBI could order disgorgement of the ₹3 lakh plus a penalty of up to ₹25 crore or three times the profit, whichever is higher.

short: A period, usually from quarter-end until results are out, when a company's insiders and their relatives may not trade its shares.
kid: Before the quiz scores are shown, the children who helped mark the papers are not allowed to make any swaps. Once everyone sees the scores, they can play again.
detail: Under SEBI's insider trading regulations, every listed company must close its trading window for designated persons, typically directors, senior staff and those handling sensitive information, and their immediate relatives, whenever they are likely to hold unpublished price sensitive information. For financial results the closure runs, under the rules as of 2025, from the end of each quarter until 48 hours after the results are made public; companies may also close it around other events such as a merger. During closure, designated persons may not trade, apart from narrow exceptions such as pre-approved trading plans. Companies announce closures to the exchanges, which is why such notices flood news feeds near quarter-end. The common confusion is to think an open window makes any trade legal: trading while actually holding unpublished information is still insider trading.
example: Say ABC Ltd's quarter ends on 30 September and results are released at 4:00 pm on 25 October. The trading window is closed from 1 October and reopens at 4:00 pm on 27 October, 48 hours after the release.

short: A privately pooled fund in India for wealthy and institutional investors, such as venture capital, private equity or hedge funds, regulated by SEBI.
kid: A group of grown-ups each put a big bag of coins into one special jar, and a helper uses it to back new lemonade stands or try clever games. Only people with lots of coins can join.
detail: An alternative investment fund (AIF) is a privately pooled vehicle registered under the SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012. Category I funds invest in areas with wider economic benefits: venture capital, angel, SME, social impact and infrastructure funds. Category II covers private equity, private credit and fund-of-funds that borrow only for day-to-day needs. Category III covers hedge-fund-style strategies that may use leverage and derivatives, including long-short funds. Under the rules as of 2025, the minimum commitment per investor is generally ₹1 crore, Category I and II funds are closed-ended with a life of at least three years, and they get tax pass-through on most income, while Category III is taxed at the fund level. Investors commit money that is drawn down over time. AIFs differ from mutual funds, which are open to the public with tight diversification rules, and from PMS, where securities sit in the client's own name.
example: Say an investor commits ₹1 crore to a Category II private equity AIF. The fund draws down 30%, or ₹30 lakh, in the first year and the remaining ₹70 lakh over the next few years as it finds deals.

short: A SEBI-registered service where a professional manages a portfolio of stocks or bonds held in the client's own name, for a high minimum investment.
kid: Instead of putting your toys in a shared toy box, you keep your own box, and a grown-up helper picks and swaps toys in it for you. You can see every toy inside.
detail: A portfolio management service (PMS) is offered by a portfolio manager registered under the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020. Unlike a mutual fund, there is no pooled scheme: securities sit in each client's own demat account, so portfolios can be tailored and every holding is visible. Services can be discretionary, where the manager decides; non-discretionary, where the client approves trades; or advisory. Under the rules as of 2025, the minimum investment is ₹50 lakh, except for accredited investors. Fees can be fixed, performance-linked with a hurdle and high-water mark, or both, and must be disclosed; SEBI also requires standardised performance reporting so returns can be compared. Because every trade happens in your own account, costs and taxes can make a PMS less efficient than a mutual fund. Do not confuse a PMS with an AIF, which pools investors' money in a fund.
example: Say a client puts ₹60 lakh into a PMS charging 20% of returns above a 10% hurdle. If the portfolio rises to ₹72 lakh in a year, the gain is ₹12 lakh, the hurdle is ₹6 lakh, and the fee is 20% of the ₹6 lakh excess, or ₹1.2 lakh.

short: An investor certified as wealthy enough to access riskier private products with lighter regulatory protection and lower minimum investments.
kid: Some rides at the fair are only for big kids who are tall enough. A grown-up checks your height and gives you a badge so you can go on them.
detail: An accredited investor is one recognised as able to understand and bear the risks of complex products, so regulators allow lighter protections. India introduced the idea in 2021. Under SEBI's rules as of 2025, individuals, HUFs and family trusts qualify with annual income of at least ₹2 crore, or net worth of at least ₹7.5 crore with at least half in financial assets, or income of ₹1 crore plus net worth of ₹5 crore with half in financial assets; companies and other trusts need net worth of ₹50 crore. Accreditation agencies approved by SEBI issue a certificate valid for a fixed period. Accredited investors can invest below the usual AIF and PMS minimums. In the US, the SEC test is mainly income above $200,000 or net worth above $1 million excluding the home. Accreditation is a wealth test, not a guarantee of skill.
example: Say an individual earns ₹1.2 crore a year and has a net worth of ₹6 crore, of which ₹3 crore is in shares and mutual funds. She fails the ₹2 crore income test and the ₹7.5 crore net-worth test but qualifies on the combined test: income above ₹1 crore, net worth above ₹5 crore and financial assets above ₹2.5 crore.

short: A person or firm licensed by SEBI to give paid, personalised investment advice, who must act in the client's interest and cannot earn sales commissions.
kid: A helper who tells you which toys suit you best gets paid only by you, not by the toy shop. So the helper has no reason to push the shop's toys.
detail: A SEBI registered investment adviser (RIA) is an individual or firm registered under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013, to give investment advice for a fee. RIAs must hold prescribed qualifications and NISM certification, assess each client's risk profile, recommend only suitable products and act in a fiduciary capacity. The core rule is separation of advice from distribution: an RIA cannot earn commissions on products it recommends, and the same family cannot be served by both its advisory and distribution arms. Under the rules as of 2025, fees charged to individual and family clients are capped by SEBI. Clients can verify registration numbers on SEBI's website. The common confusion is between an RIA and a mutual fund distributor, who is paid by fund houses through commissions, or a research analyst, who issues general recommendations. In US news, 'RIA' means an adviser registered with the SEC or a state.
example: Say an investor holds ₹40 lakh in regular mutual fund plans whose distributor commissions total about 0.8% a year, or ₹32,000. An RIA charging a flat ₹25,000 a year may move her into direct plans, so she pays the adviser instead and her yearly costs fall by ₹7,000.

short: A person or firm registered with SEBI to publish research and buy or sell recommendations on securities, with rules on disclosing conflicts of interest.
kid: A helper studies all the toys in the shop and writes notes saying which ones look good. The rules make the helper say if they own any of those toys.
detail: A SEBI registered research analyst (RA) is registered under the SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014, to prepare research reports, make buy, sell or hold recommendations, give price targets or offer opinions on listed securities. Anyone doing this for payment, including through websites, apps, Telegram groups or social media, must be registered. RAs must hold qualifications and NISM certification and disclose their holdings and conflicts in every report; under the rules as of 2025, they may not trade against their own recommendations around publication or charge individual clients above SEBI's fee limits. The key difference from an investment adviser is that research is general, not tailored to one client's finances and goals. A sell-side analyst at a broking firm is usually covered by the firm's RA registration. Unregistered sellers of stock tips act illegally even when their calls happen to be right.
example: Say an RA publishes a 'buy' on ABC Ltd at ₹480 with a target of ₹600. The implied upside is (600 - 480) / 480 = 25%, and the report must state whether the analyst or their relatives own ABC shares.

short: A social-media personality who posts about money, investing or trading, often to a large following and sometimes without any regulatory registration.
kid: Some people make fun videos telling everyone what to do with their pocket money. Some know a lot, some do not, and some are paid to say nice things about a shop.
detail: A finfluencer is a financial influencer: someone who shares content on investing, trading, loans or personal finance through YouTube, Instagram, X, Telegram and similar platforms. Many offer genuine education, but some sell stock tips, paid groups or courses, or promote products for undisclosed payment, and unregistered paid advice is illegal in India. Under SEBI's August 2024 rules, regulated entities such as brokers, mutual funds and advisers, and their agents, may not associate with unregistered persons who give advice or recommendations or make return claims, though pure education is allowed. SEBI has also ordered some finfluencers to refund large sums earned from paid tip services. For investors the checks are simple: is the person SEBI-registered as an investment adviser or research analyst, are payments and sponsorships disclosed, and are past returns verifiable? Follower count is not a credential.
example: Say an unregistered influencer charges 5,000 subscribers ₹2,000 each for a monthly tips group. That is ₹1 crore a month in fees, which SEBI could order to be refunded with penalties, since paid recommendations need registration as an adviser or research analyst.

short: A specialist appeals body in Mumbai that hears challenges to orders of SEBI and some other financial regulators, below the Supreme Court.
kid: If the playground monitor gives you a time-out and you think it is unfair, you can ask the head teacher to look again. The head teacher can agree, change it or cancel it.
detail: The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), set up under Section 15K of the SEBI Act, 1992, and based in Mumbai, hears appeals against orders of SEBI and its adjudicating officers, and of the insurance and pension regulators IRDAI and PFRDA. An appeal is generally filed within 45 days of the order. SAT can confirm, modify or set aside the order and can grant interim stays, sometimes on condition that part of a penalty is deposited. Its decisions can be challenged before the Supreme Court only on questions of law. SAT matters because it is the first independent check on a powerful regulator: its rulings have overturned or reduced several high-profile SEBI penalties and shaped how rules are read. Do not confuse a SAT stay, which pauses an order, with a final acquittal; the case continues.
example: Say SEBI fines a hypothetical broker ₹5 crore. The broker appeals to SAT within 45 days, and SAT stays the penalty on condition that 50% of it, ₹2.5 crore, is deposited while the appeal is heard.

short: An order closing a SEBI case after the accused pays an agreed sum, without admitting or denying wrongdoing.
kid: When two children argue over a broken toy, they can agree that one helps fix it and the matter is over, without deciding who broke it.
detail: A settlement order ends SEBI enforcement proceedings when the accused pays a settlement amount and sometimes accepts other terms, such as a trading ban or disgorgement, under the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018. The applicant neither admits nor denies the charges, and SEBI drops or does not start proceedings. The amount comes from a formula that weighs the type of violation, gains made, losses to investors and the applicant's history; a high-powered advisory committee and a panel of SEBI's whole-time members review each application. Serious defaults, such as fraud with market-wide impact, may be refused. Before formal settlement regulations arrived in 2014, the same idea worked through consent orders, and the older name is still used. Settlement saves time and cost for both sides, but it is not an acquittal, and SEBI can revive the case if the terms are breached.
example: Say a hypothetical listed company delayed disclosing a large order and receives a SEBI show-cause notice. It applies to settle and pays ₹48.6 lakh, and SEBI passes a settlement order closing the matter without any finding of guilt.

short: A separate segment of an Indian stock exchange where non-profits and social enterprises raise money from people who want social impact.
kid: A special corner of the market where people give coins to helpers who plant trees or teach children. They get no coins back, just a report saying how much good was done.
detail: A Social Stock Exchange (SSE) is a segment of a recognised exchange, set up in India on NSE and BSE under SEBI's 2022 framework, where social enterprises can raise funds. Not-for-profit organisations first register on the SSE and can then raise money mainly through zero coupon zero principal (ZCZP) instruments, which pay no interest and return no principal: in substance a listed donation, with the organisation required to publish an annual impact report. For-profit social enterprises can raise equity or debt through the usual routes. The SSE adds disclosure, impact audits and exchange oversight to charitable giving, which is meant to build trust and widen the donor base. The common confusion is to treat ZCZP as an investment: you get social impact and possibly a tax deduction, never your money back.
example: Say a hypothetical education charity lists an ₹80 lakh ZCZP issue on the SSE and 16 donors subscribe ₹5 lakh each. The charity receives ₹80 lakh, pays no interest, repays nothing, and must report each year how many children the money helped.

short: A special one-hour trading session Indian exchanges hold on Diwali to mark the start of the new Hindu business year, Samvat.
kid: On a festival day, families light lamps and buy something small for good luck. This is when grown-ups do the same with a tiny bit of buying, just for an hour.
detail: Muhurat trading is a symbolic session, usually about an hour long, that NSE and BSE hold on Diwali, when traders traditionally perform Lakshmi Puja and open new account books. It marks the start of a new Samvat, the Vikram Samvat Hindu calendar year that many Indian market participants use to frame the year ahead. The exchanges announce the timing each year; the session has usually been in the evening, though in 2025 it was held in the afternoon. Trades carry normal settlement obligations, so a buy is a real purchase, not a ceremony. Volumes tend to be thin and moves small, and many investors buy a token quantity for luck. Media love to report 'Samvat returns' from one Diwali to the next, but there is nothing special about that period for returns; it is a cultural milestone, not a market signal.
example: Say an investor buys 10 units of an index ETF at ₹250 during the Muhurat session, spending ₹2,500 as a token for the new Samvat. The trade settles on the next trading day like any normal purchase.

short: Settling a share trade on the same day it is made, so the buyer gets shares and the seller gets money by that evening.
kid: You swap stickers with a friend in the morning, and by evening the swap is fully done. No waiting for tomorrow.
detail: T+0 settlement means a trade is cleared and settled on the trade day itself. SEBI launched an optional T+0 cycle in India in March 2024 as a beta for 25 stocks and a few brokers, and from 2025 widened it in phases towards the top 500 stocks and all brokers, under the rules as of 2025. It runs alongside the main T+1 cycle: T+0 orders are placed in a separate morning window, at prices kept within a narrow band of the T+1 price, and funds and shares move by the evening. A planned second phase of instant, trade-by-trade settlement was put on hold. Faster settlement cuts counterparty risk and lets sellers reuse money sooner, but splitting trading between two order books can thin liquidity and widen spreads. Most trading still settles on T+1.
example: Say an investor sells 100 shares at ₹800 in the T+0 window at 11:00 am. The ₹80,000 (before charges) is settled that same evening, rather than on the next trading day under T+1.

short: A firm that keeps the official record of who owns a company's shares or a mutual fund's units, and handles allotments, transfers and payouts.
kid: In a big class, one helper keeps the list of who owns which crayons. When crayons are handed out or swapped, the helper writes it down so nobody gets mixed up.
detail: A registrar and transfer agent (RTA), registered with SEBI, maintains the register of security holders for companies and mutual funds and processes everything that changes it. For a company, the RTA handles share transfers, transmission after death, dividend and interest payments, and investor queries. As registrar to an issue, it collects IPO applications from banks and exchanges, rejects invalid ones, finalises the allotment lottery with the stock exchange, and arranges credit of shares and release of blocked funds; investors check IPO allotment status on the registrar's website. For mutual funds, RTAs process purchases, redemptions, SIPs and statements. The Indian market is concentrated: CAMS and KFin Technologies (KFintech) service most mutual fund assets, while KFintech and MUFG Intime (formerly Link Intime) handle much company registry work. RTAs keep the records; the depositories NSDL and CDSL hold the shares in demat form.
example: Say ABC Ltd's IPO has 2.5 lakh retail lots and receives 50 lakh valid retail applications. The registrar, with the stock exchange, runs a computerised lottery that gives each applicant a 1 in 20 chance, and credits one lot to each of the 2.5 lakh winners' demat accounts.

short: Illegal betting on share or commodity prices through an unregistered operator, outside any stock exchange, with no investor protection.
kid: Instead of buying a real toy from the shop, two children just bet sweets on whether the toy's price tag will go up. If the other child runs away, the sweets are gone.
detail: Dabba ('box') trading is an illegal parallel market in which an operator takes clients' orders for shares, indices or commodities but never sends them to an exchange. Instead the operator acts as the counterparty and settles profits and losses in cash, often unaccounted, based on exchange prices. Clients are drawn by high leverage, no KYC, no margin rules and no tax trail. The risks are severe: if the operator refuses to pay or disappears, there is no exchange guarantee, investor protection fund or grievance process, and participants themselves can be prosecuted. Dabba trading violates the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, and the SEBI Act, and can also attract tax and money-laundering charges. Exchanges regularly warn investors about named operators. Do not confuse it with legitimate off-market transfers, such as gifting shares to a relative through a depository.
example: Say a client 'buys' 100 shares at ₹500 through a dabba operator, without any order reaching an exchange. If the price rises to ₹530, the operator owes ₹3,000; if it falls to ₹470, the client owes ₹3,000. Either way, nothing stops the losing side from simply refusing to pay.
